data.content_ref: inline:SRC_002's perturbation-invariance diagnostic conflates checklist quality with panel reliability gain over an expert. A perturbation that satisfies checklist items while changing the outcome shows the checklist encodes correlates rather than causal features, but it does not establish that the non-expert panel is merely complying while the expert would do better. The expert's intuition could rely on the same correlates, in which case there is no reliability gain to distinguish. Conversely, if the checklist is perturbation-invariant, this proves only that the checklist tracks causal features—not that the panel using it produces more reliable judgments than the expert. The target answers 'is the checklist causally valid' rather than 'does the panel genuinely outperform the expert on average,' the comparative reliability question posed.
